@dobson4e [§2.3.2] describes model specification
as choosing two parts:
an equation linking the expected outcome to the explanatory variables,
and a probability distribution for the outcome.
For a generalized linear model,
those two parts are the three components in the solution to @exr-glm-structure:
an outcome distribution,
a linear predictor $\eta \eqdef \reglincomb$,
and a link function $g(\cdot)$ with $g(\mu) = \eta$.

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: {#exm-chronic-spec}
#### Specifying a model for the chronic medical conditions data

The outcome in @exm-chronic-eda is a count with no fixed upper limit,
so a Poisson distribution is a natural first choice.
Since a Poisson mean must be positive,
we pair the Poisson distribution with the log link
(which is also its canonical link;
see @sec-canonical-link):

$$
\ba
Y_i \mid x_i &\simind \Pois(\mu_i), \quad i = 1, \ldots, 49
\\
\logf{\mu_i} &= \eta_i
\\
\eta_i &\eqdef \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i
\ea
$$

Under this model,
$\mu_{\text{town}} \eqdef \expf{\beta_0}$ is the mean number of conditions for town women,
and $\mu_{\text{country}} \eqdef \expf{\beta_0 + \beta_1}$ is the mean for country women,
so the ratio of the two group means is

$$
\ba
\frac{\mu_{\text{country}}}{\mu_{\text{town}}}
&= \frac{\expf{\beta_0 + \beta_1}}{\expf{\beta_0}}
&& \text{(definitions of the two group means)}
\\
&= \frac{\expf{\beta_0} \expf{\beta_1}}{\expf{\beta_0}}
&& \text{(}e^{a + b} = e^a e^b\text{)}
\\
&= \expf{\beta_1}
&& \text{(cancel } \expf{\beta_0}\text{)}
\ea
$$
:::
